title: Subqueries vs Joins, EXISTS vs IN

contentBlocks.body: A subquery is a query inside another query. It can return a single value (a **scalar** subquery), a list (used with `IN`), or just answer yes/no (`EXISTS`). A **correlated** subquery refers to the outer row, so conceptually it runs once per outer row; the optimizer usually rewrites it into a join.

**Join or subquery?** Use a join when you need columns from both tables. Use `EXISTS`/`IN` when you only need to *filter* by the other table. A join to a one-to-many table repeats the parent row once per child (fan-out), so `SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ...` lists a customer with three orders three times, and people "fix" it with `DISTINCT`, which hides the mistake. `EXISTS` is a **semi-join**: each customer appears at most once.

contentBlocks.code:
-- Anti-join: customers with no paid orders
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid');

-- Same idea with LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

contentBlocks.body: `IN` and `EXISTS` behave the same for positive filters. The negations do not: `NOT IN (subquery)` returns **no rows at all** if the subquery yields a single NULL. Prefer `NOT EXISTS` for anti-joins.
Modern optimizers usually produce the same plan for `IN` and `EXISTS`. Pick the one that says what you mean, then check the plan if it is slow.

knowledgeItems.prompt: A customer has 3 paid orders. How many times does `SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id` list them?

payload.explanation: An inner join produces one row per matching pair. Use EXISTS (a semi-join) if you only want to know whether a match exists.

knowledgeItems.prompt: `orders.customer_id` contains one NULL. What does `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` return?

payload.explanation: `id <> NULL` is UNKNOWN, so the combined NOT IN predicate is never TRUE. NOT EXISTS does not have this problem.

payload.text: SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE ____ (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

knowledgeItems.prompt: Model the EXISTS and NOT EXISTS queries. Return `{ withPaidOrders, withoutPaidOrders }`, two arrays of customer names sorted by name. A customer is in the first list when at least one of their orders has status 'paid'. Each customer appears once, and orders with a null customerId never match anyone.
